title: An Ohio edge. An Iowa tossup. New CNN polls give Democrats hope in a pair of red states
content: Widespread dissatisfaction with the state of the country has opened up a prime Senate pickup opportunity for Democrats in Ohio and made for a razor-thin contest in Iowa , according to new CNN polls conducted by SSRS. President Donald Trump carried both states by double digits in 2024 , and Republicans currently hold both US Senate seats and complete control of the state government in each of them. But in these deep-red states, likely voters now mostly disapprove of Trump’s handling of the presidency, say his policies have increased the cost of living and that tariffs on foreign goods have largely been a negative for their states. About four in 10 in each state say they are financially worse off than they were two years ago. Asked which party they’d like to see in control of the Senate after this year’s midterms, Iowa’s likely voters favor the Republicans (53% to 46%). In Ohio, it’s a more even divide (52% Democrats, 48% Republicans). And in both states, Democrats have the upper hand in the race for governor. In Ohio, Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown holds a 6-point lead among likely voters over Jon Husted, a Republican former lieutenant governor who was appointed to fill the seat vacated by Vice President JD Vance. Brown is more widely known and better liked than Husted, according to the poll, and voters on both sides of the contest say their decision is more about Brown than it is about Husted. Nearly half of likely voters see Brown’s views and policies as about right ideologically, while 43% call him too liberal. Fewer are satisfied with Husted’s positions – 42% call his views and policies about right, 40% say he’s too conservative and 16% not conservative enough. Among Brown’s own supporters, 62% say that choice is more a vote for Brown than against Husted, and likewise, Husted’s voters are more anti-Brown voters (56%) than pro-Husted voters (44%). About 4 in 10 likely voters in Ohio say that which party controls the Senate will be more of a factor in their vote than the candidates’ experience and character or their positions on the issues. Voters motivated by that are split about evenly between Brown and Husted. In order to take control of the Senate, Democrats need to hold their seats in battlegrounds like Michigan, New Hampshire and Georgia while flipping four seats currently held by Republicans. The party’s best pickup opportunity comes in North Carolina, but Ohio may be their next best shot. Iowa, one of several deeply red states at the heart of this year’s Senate playing field , is more of a stretch for Democrats. The poll finds no clear leader in the Senate race in Iowa, with Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson at 45% to Democrat Josh Turek’s 43% among likely voters. Almost 3 in 10 Iowa likely voters say they haven’t yet firmly decided whom to support, and sizable shares don’t yet have an opinion on each candidate. Turek is less well-known than Hinson, with 24% saying they have never heard of him or don’t have an opinion, while 18% say the same about her. Those with an opinion of Hinson break more negative than positive, while views of Turek are about evenly split. In contrast with Ohio, most backers of both candidates in Iowa say their choices are motivated by support for their chosen candidate rather than by opposition to their opponent: 66% of Hinson supporters and 60% of Turek supporters say their choice is in support of their candidate. There are some signs in the poll that Iowa offers a better playing field for Republicans than does Ohio. In addition to likely voters’ preference for a GOP-controlled Senate, Trump’s approval rating here stands at 41% compared with 36% in Ohio and notably above his 34% average nationwide in the CNN Poll of Polls . And in assessing the candidates, more call Turek too liberal (46%) than say that Hinson is too conservative (38%). In both Iowa and Ohio, about half of likely voters call the economy and cost of living their top issue, more than 20 points higher than the second most important issue, the state of US democracy. The economic concerns that have buffeted Trump’s approval ratings nationally all year long are evident here. About three-quarters in each state say that Trump’s policies have increased the cost of living there, majorities say that increased tariffs on foreign goods are a bad thing for their state and roughly seven in 10 say they have faced at least some hardship from rising gas prices. Overall, far more say their own financial situation has worsened in the last two years than say it has gotten better. About four in 10 in each state say they are angry about the way things are going in the country today. Those angry voters express more motivation to vote than do those who are enthusiastic or satisfied with the way things are going in the country in both states. In both states, Democrats lead in the race for governor among likely voters. Democrat Rob Sand leads Republican Zach Lahn in Iowa by 9 points, while in Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton tops Republican Vivek Ramaswamy by 8 points. Both would be Democratic pickups if these margins were to hold. Impressions of Ramaswamy and Lahn appear to be weighing down their candidacies, with the share of likely voters who hold unfavorable opinions of the two Republicans outpacing favorable views by double-digit margins. By comparison, nearly half of Iowa likely voters have a favorable view of Sand – compared to 32% unfavorable – while in Ohio views of Acton are more evenly split. CNN’s Ariel Edwards-Levy, Edward Wu and Isabelle LaBianco contributed to this report.
ranking_reason: The article highlights a potential shift in political power and economic influence in two crucial states, which could have significant consequences for the national political landscape and public policy decisions.

title: She made India fall in love with women's cricket - now her era as captain is over
content: When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match but the trajectory of women's cricket in India. India went on to lose the final to England that year but women's cricket no longer remained a passing pursuit for the average Indian fan. That dogged zeal to win she infused into the team helped them lift India's first women's World Cup trophy - the same feat that had eluded them in 2017 - in emphatic fashion eight years later. Less than a year on, and within weeks of victories in the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, she has relinquished the captaincy, ending an era in which she became the team's most influential leader and one of the most recognisable figures in the sport. Star opener Smriti Mandhana, her long-time deputy, has been appointed captain across all formats. Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia, coach Amol Muzumdar, Harmanpreet and Mandhana attended the review meeting at which the leadership change was ratified. The transition, however, was not entirely seamless. Reports suggest the 37-year-old Harmanpreet was willing to relinquish the T20 captaincy immediately, but was keen to continue leading the side in One-Day Internationals and Tests so that younger players could benefit from her experience. The BCCI, however, was intent on a younger person at the helm and opted for the 30-year-old Mandhana. In some ways, the move mirrors the BCCI's decision to replace Suryakumar Yadav as captain of the men's T20 side shortly after India won the World Cup earlier this year, with the captaincy passing to Shreyas Iyer. Harmanpreet's future as captain had become a subject of intense debate in cricketing circles after India's below-par performance at the T20 World Cup in England a few months ago. Her own poor form with the bat amplified concerns and prompted the BCCI to consider changes that could help the team meet the growing challenges of a women's game that continues to expand rapidly around the world. Approaching her 38th birthday, and after almost a decade at the helm, Harmanpreet found herself under increasing scrutiny as her form dipped. Opinion on whether she should continue as captain was sharply divided among former women players and captains. Former cricketer Diana Edulji, among the most respected names in the game, felt Harmanpreet had done everything that could reasonably have been expected of her and that it was time for a younger captain to take over. Former captain Anjum Chopra, meanwhile, argued that Harmanpreet's experience remained invaluable and that she should stay on. Sensing that the BCCI was strongly inclined towards a change, Harmanpreet opted to step down during the review meeting. She later announced her decision in an emotional Instagram post. "I feel I have done my duty. I gave this team everything I had," she wrote. "Now, it is time for me to turn the page… Blood. Sweat. Sacrifice. Pride. I gave it all. Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again. "Captaincy ends, the journey continues." Harmanpreet's intention to continue playing now leaves the BCCI with another decision to make about her future. In Suryakumar Yadav's case, he not only lost the captaincy but also his place in India's T20 side. Given the depth of talent available in the men's game, it was easier for Ajit Agarkar and his fellow selectors to take what was always likely to be a contentious decision. The situation in the women's game is different. Despite Harmanpreet's modest recent form, replacing a player of her experience and stature may not be straightforward, as the talent pipeline is not yet as deep as it is in men's cricket. Whatever the future holds, Harmanpreet has scripted among the more memorable careers in women's cricket. Spanning more than two decades, it is a journey marked by significant achievements and milestones. Born into a family of modest means in Punjab's Moga city, Harmanpreet developed a passion for cricket at an early age. Her family's support was vital in the early years, but her rise to national recognition came after she joined the Railways - a transition facilitated by Diana Edulji - and moved to Mumbai. The superior facilities and greater professionalism associated with Mumbai's sporting culture helped accelerate her development. She made her India debut in 2009 at the age of 20 and has remained an integral part of the national side across formats ever since. An all-rounder for the better part of her first decade in cricket, she made herself indispensable to the side with her explosive middle-order batting, crafty off-spin and sharp fielding skills. Her blistering century against Australia in the semi-final of the 2017 Women's ODI World Cup remains one of the defining knocks in the history of the women's game. India went on to lose to England in the final, but beating Australia was a monumental hurdle overcome. That century also helped spark wider interest in women's cricket in India, and transformed Harmanpreet into a household name. The second decade of her career showcased her prowess both as batter and captain. Having succeeded Mithali Raj as T20 captain in 2016, Harmanpreet assumed charge across all formats in 2022 and went on to guide India to some of the greatest successes in its history. Her leadership was marked by an aggressive pursuit of victory. That fearless approach instilled confidence and ambition in her teammates, helping the team overcome even the previously unbeatable Australians, most memorably in the semi-final of the 2025 ODI World Cup. Unlike in 2017, Harmanpreet couldn't get a hundred on that occasion, but her innings of 89 was a stellar effort as captain. Combined with Jemimah Rodrigues's century, it helped India secure a famous victory over their arch rivals. India then defeated South Africa in the final to reach what many regard as the pinnacle of achievement in the history of Indian women's cricket. With multiple titles and trophies won under her leadership, Harmanpreet leaves behind a formidable legacy for her successor, Smriti Mandhana, to emulate. The 73-year-old has been arrested over allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations. Opposition leaders allege that CEC Gyanesh Kumar manipulated voter rolls to favour PM Narendra Modi's party. As a result, Toyama city may have received more funding from the central government than it should have. A sharp increase in human activity is affecting the way the Himalayan monal lives and communicates, studies show. Relatives are finding themselves with no compensation and facing an administrative nightmare. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. ranking_reason: The change in captaincy may have significant implications for the future of Indian women's cricket and the public's perception of the sport.

title: Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests dies
content: An elderly woman whose eviction sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis and a political row that triggered early elections has died, according to Madrid's tenants union. Maricarmen Abascal, 87, was forcibly removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years on 23 September after she was unable to afford steep rent increases. The company that owned the flat later offered to allow her to return at a lower rate - but she was unable to sign an agreement as she had been admitted to hospital. Announcing her death, Madrid Tenants' Union said Abascal's situation marked "a turning point in the history of this country". The 87-year-old and her eviction became a symbol for Spain's housing crisis. The Socialist-led government sought to respond to the protests but its bid to push through urgent housing measures failed, prompting Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call snap elections. "Speculation costs lives, and today rent profiteering has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen," said union spokeswoman Alicia del Río. "Her memory lives on and makes us fight even harder." The 87-year-old was already in fragile health at the time of her eviction and she was admitted to Madrid's Gregorio Marañón Hospital, sending messages of support to protesters from her hospital bed. When news of her death reached Puerta del Sol - the Madrid square where thousands have camped since her eviction to demand more affordable housing - there was a collective gasp, followed by a minute of silence. Dozens of candles were lit around the square, with more laid out to form an altar to Abascal in front of the headquarters of the Community of Madrid government. Messages laid at the scene read "it's not a death, it's a killing", "the fight will continue" and "Maricarmen, the grandmother of the whole country", among others. Maricarmen Abascal's father had first rented the flat in Madrid's Retiro district in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent. The area has become increasingly sought-after, and Urbagestión, the company that bought the property in 2018, increased the rent from €500 per month (£428; $572) to €2,650 (£2,280; $3,020). Rental costs in Madrid have soared by more than 100% over the last decade, according to property site Idealista. The company later offered to reduce this to €1,650 - still €300 more than Abascal's monthly pension. Three earlier attempts to evict her had been blocked by the courts and her case attracted widespread support from the public and celebrities. Prime Minister Sánchez's minority government announced two emergency decrees to tackle the housing crisis, but they were rejected in Congress last week , and on Monday he called elections for 29 November. Opponents pointed out he had had eight years in office to respond to the issue. Tens of thousands of people took to the streets last weekend in cities across the country, as protests continued. "All my love goes to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Sánchez said on Wednesday night. "A hug as well to everyone who today feels this loss as their own." The leader of the opposition People's Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, also sent his condolences, appealing for her death not to be politicised: "No campaign, no parties, no self-interested exploitation. No more stones in the wall. "In the face of a person's death, only respect is in order," he added. The Madrid Tenants' Union said the events surrounding her eviction represented a turning point in the country's history, but added that the cost to get to this point had been "too high". In one video recorded from her hospital bed following her eviction, Maricarmen said: "I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs." A few hundred people marched from Puerta del Sol to parliament on Wednesday night, chanting "we will not tolerate a single eviction more" and "the fight will continue, Maricarmen is still alive". There were other chants against the police. Many protesters believed that police had been complicit in the evictions, as under court orders they have to remove tenants who have been served eviction notices. After a couple of hours, the chants near Congress gave way to another minute of silence. Then, a big collective shout of "murderers". One protester told the BBC that people would remain in the square "as long as necessary". Earlier on Wednesday, unions had called a general strike to take place on 11 November, demanding housing reforms. The public outcry over Abascal's situation exposed the deep political divisions in Spain. The political right argued that the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further. Sánchez said on Monday he needed "a broader progressive majority" that could "overcome the resistance of the elites" to push through reforms. However, other issues unrelated to housing, including numerous corruption scandals linked to his party, and pressures relating to the cost of living and immigration, have also caused him problems. Most opinion polls suggest the conservative People's Party is likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party, currently third in the polls, to form a government. Additional reporting by Tom McArthur Copyright 2026 BBC. ranking_reason: The death of Maricarmen Abascal serves as a powerful reminder of the human cost of Spain's housing crisis and the need for urgent reform.

analysis.reason: The death of Maricarmen Abascal serves as a powerful reminder of the human cost of Spain's housing crisis and the need for urgent reform.
